result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.lowest_common_ancestor()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find the lowest common ancestor of two nodes in a DAG. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L37763-L37841){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.lowest_common_ancestor( node_1, node_2, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Lowest common ancestor](/assets/graphs/lowest-common-ancestor.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A seven-node DAG with the query nodes E and F outlined. A, B, and D all have paths to both, but D is the closest, so it is the lowest common ancestor, shown in the accent color with its edges to E and F. The card lists the common ancestors A, B, D and the answer D." width="100%"} A common ancestor of two nodes is a node with a path to both. The *lowest* common ancestor (LCA) is the one closest to them: no other common ancestor lies below it. In a taxonomy or phylogeny this is the most specific group the two share (the most recent common ancestor); in version control, the merge base of two branches; in an organization chart, the first manager both people report to. As is usual for LCAs, a node counts as its own ancestor, so if one node is an ancestor of the other, it is the answer. A general DAG can have several lowest common ancestors (in a tree there is exactly one); in that case the deepest one, measured by its longest path from a source, is returned, with ties going to the lowest node ID. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [node_1]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The first node, as an integer ID or a string label. [node_2]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The second node, as an integer ID or a string label. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The ID of the lowest common ancestor, or `None` if the two nodes have no common ancestor. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If a label does not exist, or the graph is undirected or contains a cycle. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} In this small taxonomy, cats and dogs meet at Carnivora, while a cat and a mouse only meet at Mammalia: ::: {#25fa0939 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec tree = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["Mammalia", "Carnivora", "Rodentia", "cat", "dog", "mouse"]) .add_edges([ ("Mammalia", "Carnivora"), ("Mammalia", "Rodentia"), ("Carnivora", "cat"), ("Carnivora", "dog"), ("Rodentia", "mouse"), ]) ) label = tree.get_label_from_id label(tree.lowest_common_ancestor("cat", "dog")), label( tree.lowest_common_ancestor("cat", "mouse") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ('Carnivora', 'Mammalia') ``` ::: :::
